impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions by comparing function calls in an emulator to a model are abstract under step one of the Alice framework for patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia, holding that the asserted claims of the '322 and '115 patents are directed to an abstract idea at Alice step one and remanding for step two analysis. The court also held that damages based on Norton's foreign sales were improperly awarded, as the patent statute does not have extraterritorial reach for such sales.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies defending against patent assertions involving software and cybersecurity methods gain a stronger basis to challenge eligibility under § 101. The foreign-sales damages ruling limits patentees' ability to recover damages for sales made outside the United States.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the software and cybersecurity space face heightened risk that their claims will be deemed abstract under Alice step one, potentially invalidating significant patent portfolios.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting JMOL that Teva's headache patent claims covering humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity of Teva's anti-CGRP migraine treatment patents, reinstating the jury's verdict that Lilly willfully infringed and that the claims were not invalid. The case involves patents covering the active ingredient in Teva's Ajovy product and Lilly's competing migraine treatments.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders benefit from the court's more permissive view of written description and enablement for antibody claims, reinforcing the viability of genus claims in biologics patents where the specification discloses known methods for making the claimed antibodies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face strengthened patent barriers in the migraine treatment market and potentially in broader biologics litigation, as genus antibody claims are harder to invalidate under § 112.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether sufficient evidence supported the jury's finding that each of the four asserted trade secrets was a protectable trade secret under California law, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the trade secret misappropriation verdict, holding plaintiffs failed to prove their asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed the patent invalidity finding for the same reason—Dr. Elist's contribution of generally known ideas could not constitute inventive contribution. The counterfeiting claim was affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from a strengthened requirement that plaintiffs must demonstrate the information claimed as a trade secret is not generally known in the field, providing a clearer defense pathway.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection for product designs and methods face heightened evidentiary burdens to establish that their claimed secrets are not already known in the industry.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality grounds where accused processor design and testing occurs abroad, and whether VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory was properly rejected.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed-in-part the grant of summary judgment to Intel on extraterritoriality grounds for the '836 patent relating to multicore processor task assignment, finding that VLSI raised genuine disputes of material fact regarding domestic infringement. The court affirmed the rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory and the striking of certain damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement against semiconductor companies with global operations benefit from the court's rejection of broad extraterritoriality defenses where there is evidence of domestic use or testing of accused products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global design and manufacturing operations may face continued infringement exposure in the U.S. even when significant accused activities occur abroad, and must carefully manage discovery disclosures for damages theories.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge for summary judgment purposes, and whether source code constitutes hearsay under the Federal Rules of Evidence in the context of the on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the pre-AIA on-sale bar, holding that 30(b)(6) deposition testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the corporate designee lacks personal knowledge, and that computer source code commands are not hearsay statements. The ruling invalidated claims relating to engine controller reprogramming technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants challenging patent validity benefit from expanded admissibility of corporate designee testimony and source code evidence, making it easier to prove prior art sales and technical functionality at summary judgment.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges, as competitors can more readily use corporate representative testimony and source code to establish pre-critical-date sales of prior art products.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether genuine disputes of material fact precluded summary judgment on inequitable conduct and Walker Process antitrust fraud claims relating to Tenaris's failure to disclose prior art CYMAX documents during patent prosecution.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on both inequitable conduct (which had been granted against Tenaris) and Walker Process fraud (which had been granted in favor of Tenaris), finding genuine disputes of material fact on both issues. The case involves coiled tubing patents where the applicants acquired prior art documents from a predecessor company but allegedly failed to disclose them to the PTO.
impacts.positiveImplications: Competitors challenging patents obtained through allegedly inequitable conduct retain their ability to pursue both patent unenforceability and antitrust claims where factual disputes exist about the patentee's intent and materiality of withheld references.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who acquire prior art materials through corporate acquisitions face ongoing litigation risk if they fail to disclose those materials during prosecution, with potential exposure to both inequitable conduct and Walker Process antitrust liability.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement retains sufficient exclusionary rights to establish Article III standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who retain the right to sue for infringement in a license agreement possess sufficient exclusionary rights to satisfy constitutional standing requirements, even after granting an exclusive commercialization license to another party.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring license agreements can retain standing to enforce their patents by reserving the right to sue for infringement, allowing flexible commercialization arrangements while maintaining enforcement capability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a standing-based defense when the patent owner has expressly retained suit rights in the license agreement, even if most commercial rights have been exclusively licensed to a third party.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated eligibility rulings for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents relating to non-uniform constellations used in digital TV broadcasting, finding those claims may be directed to abstract mathematical concepts, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents that recite specific hardware implementations. The court also affirmed the infringement and damages findings against LG.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders whose claims recite specific hardware implementations of mathematical or algorithmic innovations in communications standards retain strong eligibility positions. The affirmation of damages also supports robust royalty theories for standard-essential-type patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing digital communications standards face continued patent infringement exposure for hardware-implemented claims, while patent holders with purely method-based claims covering mathematical optimizations face renewed § 101 challenges.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action after having missed the statutory deadline to seek a stay of its original declaratory judgment action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay under § 1659(a) by dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action. BioMarin was barred from obtaining a stay of Ascendis's patent non-infringement action because it missed the 30-day deadline in the original proceeding.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and life sciences companies filing declaratory judgment actions of non-infringement can proceed with district court litigation without facing mandatory stays when ITC respondents attempt procedural gamesmanship by refiling to reset statutory deadlines.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who fail to timely seek a mandatory stay of parallel district court proceedings lose that tactical option permanently and cannot reset the clock through dismissal and refiling strategies.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC properly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement features violated Section 337 by infringing Masimo's wearable pulse oximetry patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing and selling Apple Watches that infringed Masimo's wearable blood oxygen measurement patents, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing models. The court found no error in the domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with validated wearable technology patents gain confidence in ITC enforcement as a viable mechanism to block importation of infringing consumer electronics products, even against the largest technology companies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies face significant supply chain and product design risks when ITC exclusion orders are affirmed, potentially requiring costly redesigns or removal of features from products already in the market.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a patent damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy where the patentee's damages expert used a flawed methodology.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report in a patent infringement case against Microsoft involving Azure cloud networking technology, finding the district court applied an overly stringent standard. The court vacated the summary judgment that had been granted based solely on the absence of an admissible damages theory.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent plaintiffs benefit from a more permissive standard for admissibility of damages expert testimony, reducing the risk that methodological imperfections will result in total exclusion and summary judgment for defendants.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending patent cases face reduced ability to obtain summary judgment by attacking the admissibility of damages expert reports, as courts must distinguish between flawed methodology warranting exclusion and imperfect but admissible opinions.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund expenses unrelated to PACER operations, and whether incentive awards to class representatives were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of the $125 million PACER fee class action settlement, upholding the district court's findings that the settlement was fair and that hundreds of thousands of PACER users would be fully or substantially reimbursed. The court also affirmed attorneys' fee awards and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives.
impacts.positiveImplications: The approval of incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives affirms that service awards remain permissible in class action settlements, providing continued incentive for organizational plaintiffs to bring public-interest class litigation.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether the patentee was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents by Mylan's generic drug, holding that the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' must be measured at the standard temperature used in the pharmaceutical field. The court also upheld the bar on Actelion's doctrine of equivalents theory.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers benefit from the court's construction requiring pH measurements at field-standard temperatures, potentially clearing the way for generic versions of epoprostenol (Veletri) to enter the market.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies with composition patents that specify pH parameters face narrower claim scope when measurement conditions are construed according to industry-standard practices rather than conditions that might favor infringement findings.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination for claims involving time-delayed reporting of sensor information in logistics tracking systems, and whether a non-party to district court litigation may file IPR petitions on behalf of or in coordination with a time-barred party.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's finding that challenged claims of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent were unpatentable as obvious, remanding for further proceedings. The case raised significant questions about whether Qualcomm, which was not a party to the underlying district court litigation, improperly filed IPR petitions on behalf of the time-barred defendant Roambee.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners gain protection against potential circumvention of the IPR time bar where third parties file petitions on behalf of or in coordination with parties who have missed the statutory filing deadline.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to use IPR as a defense strategy face scrutiny if they coordinate with or act as proxies for time-barred parties, potentially limiting the availability of post-grant challenges to competitors' patents.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may correct patent inventorship under 35 U.S.C. § 256(b) when the patent owner cannot locate an omitted co-inventor, and whether the patents are invalid for incorrect inventorship when correction cannot be obtained through § 256(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that patents listing incorrect inventorship are invalid where the patent owner cannot locate an omitted co-inventor to obtain consent for correction under § 256(a), and the district court declined to order correction under § 256(b). The ruling affects companies that collaborate with foreign manufacturers whose employees contribute to inventions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can use inventorship defects as a strong invalidity defense when patent owners have failed to properly identify and track all contributors to an invention, particularly in global supply chain collaborations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies collaborating with foreign manufacturers on product development face significant patent validity risks if they fail to document and maintain contact with all potential co-inventors, as inability to locate an omitted inventor may render the patent invalid.
